catalog_quote: I propose that English stress is both listed in the lexicon and derived by rule ... English verbs and unsuffixed adjectives. These words receive final stress if they end in a string of at least two consonants or with a syllable having a long vowel, otherwise penultimate stress, as in (23): obey torment astonish / atone usurp develop ... the criterion for prominence in word-final syllables (at least in these words) is different from the one that prevails nonfinally, which (as we shall see) is simply the distinction between branching and nonbranching rhymes. ... (25) English Stress Rule: At the right edge of a word, form a maximally binary foot on the rhyme projection ... Label feet s w. ... The stress pattern of nouns is somewhat different. Here, the final syllable always receives stress if it contains a long vowel: (28) Manitou cavalcade misanthrope ... The final syllable also sometimes…
sweep_summary: Seven title hits for English; none changes the catalog's weight-hedged coding from Hayes 1982. Peck 1971 (Kivung 4(3)) was located in the LLM/Kivung open archive, fetched sources (pp. 194-207; pp. 192-193 missing from the scan) and scanned: it is a review of Vanderslice's rules for assigning sentence accent and intonation to text and presupposes dictionary-listed word stress, so it is silent on placement. Peperkamp 1997 (dissertation, print only) and 1996 (Kleinhenz volume, paywalled; Glottolog's '1966'/'Acta Linguistica Hafniensia' are errors) are about prosodic words and clitics in Romance/Dutch, judged from the author's open GLOT 1999 summary and abstracts. Aitken 1984 and Petyt 1985 use 'accent' in the regional-pronunciation sense (not relevant). Pike 1945 (intonation-marking procedure in Fries's ESL manual) is on archive.org only as restricted lending; Hayes 1995 (already listed) has no open copy and would only restate Hayes 1982. No new authoritative stress statement found; nothing to acquire at high priority.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the secondary-rule quote (p. 243), the domain quote (p. 264) and the heavy-syllable criterion are all verbatim in the held author-hosted PDF of Hayes 1982 at the stated pages (pp. 237-239 for the deciding splice; locator says 237-240). (2) Deciding source: a primary, authoritative 1982 Linguistic Inquiry phonology article by a leading metrical phonologist, with explicit rules and full example sets; it is the published form of the dissertation chapter StressTyp2 itself quotes. The qs-tier pipeline's read/verify/adjudicate/V-recheck trail (A,B,C,E) is intact and the V readers confirmed 20 forms against page images. sources.citation: Peck, Charles W. 1971. The placement of accent in English (review article of Vanderslice's rules for assigning prosody to text). Kivung 4(3): 192-207. (Glottolog 71452)
sources.quote: p. 200: "Many other words have two heavy syllables, only one of which is accentable. The following words have two heavy syllables, the second one of which is ordinarily unaccentable. These are called 'falling stress' words. 'ver_ti,go 'ob_fus,cate 'can,not 'fruc_ti,fy 'black,bird 'op_e,ra_tor 'nit,wit 'sky,scra_per. In the following words, the first heavy syllable is unaccentable. Such words are called 'rising stress' words. ,com_pen'sa_tion ,ob_ser'va_tion ,con_fi_gu'ra_tion ,or_ien'ta_tion" — p. 204: "the canonical forms of the words could have been obtained from a dictionary."
sources.locator: p. 200 (Rule IIE, rhythm rule) and p. 204
sources.note: A review article presenting Vanderslice's rules for assigning sentence-level ACCENT, CADENCE, ENDGLIDE, rhythm-rule reduction and de-accenting of echoic elements to running text (an early text-to-speech prosody algorithm). Word-level stress is taken as given: each word's 'canonical form' (heavy accentable / heavy unaccentable / light syllables, 'falling stress' vs 'rising stress' words) is assumed to come from a dictionary; no rule for where lexical stress falls is stated. Archive scan holds pp. 194-207 (pp. 192-193 missing; title block pasted onto p. 194); scanned.
